title: Immunization: Use the Current Canadian Schedule
bottomLine: Canadian vaccine recommendations change faster than memorized schedules. Use the current Canadian Immunization Guide and NACI statement plus the patient's provincial or territorial program, then apply age, pregnancy, immune status, medical risk, travel, exposure and prior-dose history.
recognize: Vaccination is lifelong; adult risk assessment includes routine and risk-based vaccines rather than childhood records alone.
Pregnancy changes both indications and contraindications; some vaccines are specifically recommended during pregnancy while live vaccines are generally avoided.
Immunocompromised patients may need additional doses or alternative schedules and may not be candidates for certain live vaccines.
differentiate: A product being authorized in Canada is not the same as NACI recommending it for every person or a province publicly funding it.
Minor illness and many stable chronic conditions are not reasons to defer routine immunization.
assessment: Review vaccine record, age, pregnancy, immune status, splenic function, chronic disease, travel, occupation, outbreak or exposure history and previous severe vaccine reaction.
Ask about access barriers and offer catch-up rather than restarting a series unnecessarily.
workup: Serologic testing is not routinely required before or after most vaccines; use it only for defined indications.
Check current NACI and Canadian Immunization Guide guidance when product availability or recommendations have changed.
management: Give indicated vaccines at the same visit when permitted and use catch-up principles rather than missed-opportunity deferral.
The Canadian Immunization Guide was updated repeatedly in 2026, including influenza 2026–27, RSV guidance, pneumococcal product changes and multiple vaccine chapters.
medicationSafety: Screen for true contraindications such as anaphylaxis to a component and relevant live-vaccine contraindications; do not label expected local or systemic reactions as vaccine allergy.
Timing around immunosuppressive therapy, blood products and selected biologics requires current guidance.
redFlags: Possible vaccine-preventable disease requiring public-health action
Immunocompromised patient being considered for live vaccine
Pregnancy with exposure to a vaccine-preventable infection
counselling: Use presumptive, respectful recommendations and address specific concerns with evidence rather than overwhelming the patient with generic facts.
Explain the difference between national recommendation and local public funding when relevant.
followUp: Document immunization as required and schedule outstanding doses; report adverse events following immunization through the applicable provincial or territorial process.
examTrap: Using an old memorized adult pneumococcal or RSV schedule instead of checking the current Canadian Immunization Guide.
oneLinePearl: On Canadian vaccine questions, current NACI guidance beats memory.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada Canadian Immunization Guide

title: Preventive Screening: Risk, Evidence, and Local Programs
bottomLine: Screening is for people without symptoms; symptomatic patients need diagnostic evaluation. Use current Canadian evidence plus provincial or territorial programs, and individualize when high-risk features move a patient outside average-risk guidance.
recognize: Cancer screening schedules can differ by province and territory because programs, tests and implementation vary.
In June 2026, PHAC launched the National Advisory Committee on Preventive Health Services to replace the former Canadian Task Force and develop national preventive-care guidance.
Over-screening can cause false positives, overdiagnosis, complications and inequitable resource use.
differentiate: Screening tests have eligibility rules; a new symptom is not managed by simply ordering the screening test.
Screening should stop or change when expected benefit is outweighed by competing illness, limited life expectancy or patient preference.
assessment: Clarify symptoms first, then age, anatomy, smoking history, family or genetic risk, prior screening results, immunocompromise and access barriers.
Ask whether the patient can complete follow-up after an abnormal screen before ordering it.
workup: Use the province or territory's current screening pathway and current national evidence; do not invent a universal Canada-wide interval when implementation differs.
management: Offer evidence-supported screening using shared decision-making where benefits and harms are preference-sensitive.
Abnormal screening results require diagnostic follow-up and ownership; the screening program is not the endpoint.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary premedication or invasive testing before a screening result actually warrants it.
counselling: Explain absolute benefit, false-positive and overdiagnosis potential and what an abnormal result would mean.
Address transportation, language, disability and other access barriers.
followUp: Track abnormal screens until definitive diagnostic resolution and update recall intervals after prior abnormalities.
examTrap: Ordering a routine screening test for a symptomatic patient instead of switching to a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms means screening; symptoms mean diagnosis.
sourceBasis: PHAC National Advisory Committee on Preventive Health Services 2026
Provincial and Territorial Cancer Screening Programs

title: Antimicrobial Stewardship: Treat Infection, Not Anxiety
bottomLine: Before prescribing an antimicrobial, name the infection syndrome, estimate bacterial probability and severity, obtain cultures when they will change care, choose the narrowest effective agent and define dose, duration, reassessment and stop or de-escalation criteria.
recognize: Viral respiratory syndromes, asymptomatic bacteriuria and noninfectious inflammation are common reasons antibiotics are overused.
Recent antibiotics, hospitalization, resistant-organism history and local antibiogram change empiric choices.
Source control can matter more than broader antibiotics in abscess, obstructed infection, infected device or biliary or urinary obstruction.
differentiate: Colonization is not infection; a positive culture without a compatible syndrome may not need treatment.
Broad-spectrum therapy may be appropriate initially in severe sepsis, but should be narrowed when evidence permits.
assessment: Assess severity or organ dysfunction, likely source, allergy history, renal and hepatic function, pregnancy, immune status, prior cultures and recent antimicrobials.
Verify whether a reported beta-lactam allergy is a true immediate or severe reaction versus intolerance or a remote label.
workup: Obtain cultures before antibiotics when feasible in severe infection without delaying life-saving treatment; avoid cultures when a positive result is likely to represent colonization and will not change care.
management: Use Canadian, provincial and local guidance and antibiograms; choose the shortest evidence-supported effective duration.
Review therapy when cultures or results return and de-escalate, stop or switch route when clinically appropriate.
medicationSafety: Check renal dosing, QT risk, C. difficile risk, interactions and pregnancy considerations.
Unnecessary antibiotics expose patients to adverse drug events and antimicrobial resistance without benefit.
counselling: Explain why an antibiotic is not indicated in a way that validates symptoms and offers a symptom-care and return plan.
followUp: Set a review point for cultures and clinical response; persistent or worsening symptoms require diagnostic reassessment, not automatic broadening.
examTrap: Treating a culture result rather than the patient or extending antibiotic duration just to be safe without evidence.
oneLinePearl: Antibiotics need a syndrome, a target, and a stop plan.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship recommendations

title: Sepsis: Recognize Organ Dysfunction Early
bottomLine: Sepsis is infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction. Do not wait for fever, hypotension or a positive culture: recognize new organ dysfunction, begin resuscitation and antibiotics, and obtain source control.
recognize: Older and immunocompromised patients may be afebrile or hypothermic.
Tachycardia alone is nonspecific; concern rises when infection is paired with altered mentation, hypoxemia, oliguria, poor perfusion or other organ dysfunction.
Septic shock is a high-risk subset requiring vasopressors despite adequate volume resuscitation.
differentiate: Shock may be hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive or distributive; bedside reassessment prevents reflex fluid overload.
A lactate elevation is a risk and perfusion marker, not proof of bacterial infection by itself.
assessment: ABCs, mental status, perfusion, BP, oxygenation, urine output, likely source, comorbidity and goals of care.
Look for source-control emergencies such as obstructed urinary or biliary tract, abscess, infected device or necrotizing infection.
workup: Obtain cultures and source-directed labs or imaging before antibiotics when feasible without harmful delay; trend perfusion markers when they guide resuscitation.
management: Begin appropriate empiric antimicrobials promptly in suspected sepsis or shock, give crystalloid guided by perfusion and fluid responsiveness, and use norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor for persistent septic shock in monitored acute care.
Reassess after each intervention and arrange urgent source control when required.
De-escalate antimicrobials when microbiology and clinical data permit.
medicationSafety: Large fixed fluid volumes can harm patients with heart or renal failure; resuscitation must be reassessed dynamically.
Vasopressors require monitored administration and ischemia or extravasation vigilance.
counselling: After recovery, discuss medication changes, infection source and post-sepsis functional or cognitive symptoms when relevant.
followUp: Transitions should include culture results, antimicrobial duration, source-control follow-up and review of medications held during sepsis.
examTrap: Waiting for culture confirmation before treating suspected infection with worsening organ dysfunction.
oneLinePearl: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction; treat while you prove the source.
